title: H-1B for Entrepreneurs: How to Self-Sponsor Your Visa Through Your Own Startup
excerpt: The H-1B Modernization Rule now lets founders sponsor themselves through their own companies — but USCIS demands specific corporate structures, specialty occupation proof, and prevailing wage compliance to approve the petition.
body:
• The H-1B Modernization Final Rule, effective January 17, 2025, explicitly allows entrepreneurs to self-sponsor H-1B visas through companies they own — even with 100% ownership — replacing the old employer-employee relationship test with a "bona fide job offer" standard.
  • Founders must demonstrate a specialty occupation role tied to a specific degree, pay themselves the prevailing wage through formal payroll (not equity), and maintain a detailed business plan with financial projections.
  • USCIS requires a formalized corporate structure — such as a board of directors or investor group with authority to hire, supervise, and terminate the founder — to establish employer control distinct from ownership.
  • Initial approvals for entrepreneur-sponsored H-1Bs are limited to 18 months (not the standard three years), and USCIS has expanded site visit authority to verify that work matches the petition.

For years, the question haunted every H-1B holder with a business idea: can you transfer your visa to a company you founded? The answer was technically yes, but the path was so riddled with ambiguity that most immigration attorneys counselled against it. That changed on January 17, 2025, when the Department of Homeland Security implemented the H-1B Modernization Final Rule — the most significant overhaul of the program in over a decade.

The rule explicitly acknowledges that startup founders can hold H-1B status through their own companies. It replaces the old requirement to prove an outside party controlled the founder's employment with a clearer standard: demonstrate a bona fide business, a specialty occupation role, and prevailing wage compliance.

What Changed: From Employer-Employee Test to Bona Fide Job Offer

Under previous USCIS policy, the core obstacle was the "right to control" test. If you owned the company filing your H-1B petition, USCIS questioned whether a genuine employer-employee relationship existed. How could you be both boss and employee? Founders who held majority stakes routinely received Requests for Evidence (RFEs) challenging this structure, and many petitions were denied.

The Modernization Rule shifts the framework. According to analysis published by Fragomen, the rule moves "from proving an employer-employee relationship to establishing a bona fide job offer." USCIS now evaluates whether the company is a real, operating business and whether the position requires specialized skills — not whether the founder has an arm's-length employment arrangement with themselves.

Immigration law firm Wildes & Weinberg confirmed this shift works in practice, announcing the approval of an H-1B for an entrepreneur who was the "sole member of his startup entity" under the new rules. The firm noted it demonstrated a valid employer-employee relationship by providing "robust evidence of the client's qualifying investment in the operating company."

Key Requirements: What USCIS Demands From Founder-Petitioners

"Founders who held majority stakes routinely received Requests for Evidence (RFEs) challenging this structure, and many petitions were denied.</p> <p>The Modernization Rule shifts the framework."

Self-sponsorship is now permitted, but it is not a rubber stamp. According to guidance from Reddy Neumann Brown PC, founders must satisfy several specific requirements:

Specialty occupation role. The founder's position must require at least a bachelor's degree in a specific field. A CTO performing specialized engineering work qualifies. A founder doing general management and administration likely does not. USCIS scrutinizes whether the role involves "specific expertise and job functions tied to a degree in a relevant field," as the American Visa Law Group notes.

Bona fide business documentation. At minimum, founders must provide a Federal Employer Identification Number (FEIN), articles of incorporation, bylaws or an operating agreement, business licenses, a business bank account, and payroll setup. A detailed business plan with 12–24 month financial projections, market analysis, and evidence of funding significantly strengthens the petition.

Prevailing wage through payroll. This is non-negotiable. Founders must pay themselves the prevailing wage listed on the Labor Condition Application through standard payroll with taxes withheld. Equity stakes and "sweat equity" do not satisfy H-1B wage requirements.

Formalized corporate governance. According to the Michigan Bar Journal's analysis of the final rule, founders can qualify if they demonstrate "a board of directors or investor group with the authority to hire, supervise, and terminate the H-1B beneficiary, a contractual employment agreement outlining work duties, salary, and reporting structures, or operational independence, ensuring that the startup entity exercises distinct employer control." In practice, this means having at least one independent board member or investor who can exercise oversight over the founder's employment.

The 18-Month Cap and Other Guardrails

The Modernization Rule includes specific safeguards for entrepreneur-sponsored petitions. Initial approvals are limited to 18 months, not the standard three-year validity period. The first extension is also capped at 18 months. Only subsequent extensions may be approved for the full three-year term. DHS described these limitations as "a safeguard against possible fraudulent petitions."

USCIS has also expanded its site visit authority under the Administrative Site Visit and Verification Program. Officers may visit the listed office location to confirm the founder is performing the specialty occupation work described in the petition, that the company is operational, and that wage and working conditions match LCA attestations.

Common Pitfalls That Sink Entrepreneur Petitions

Immigration attorneys flag several recurring mistakes. Describing the role in terms of ownership rather than job duties is the most common — USCIS wants to see a position description that reads like a job posting, not a cap table entry. Failing to establish payroll before filing is another red flag; bank transfers to yourself without proper withholding and W-2 documentation will trigger an RFE or denial.

The American Visa Law Group has also warned about "bogus startups" — individuals creating shell companies solely to maintain visa status. USCIS has limited capacity to assess business plan viability, but a company with no clients, no revenue trajectory, and no demonstrable operations will face heightened scrutiny.

Founders must also remember they still need to be selected in the annual H-1B lottery unless their petition is cap-exempt. One workaround: securing concurrent H-1B employment through a cap-exempt entity (such as a university or nonprofit research institution) while simultaneously holding a cap-subject H-1B with their own startup.

Why This Matters for the Indian Diaspora

Indian nationals hold the largest share of H-1B visas — roughly 72% of approvals in recent years — and face the longest green card backlogs, often exceeding a decade. For thousands of Indian-origin professionals in the United States, the Modernization Rule creates a practical alternative to remaining indefinitely dependent on a single corporate employer for immigration status.

The ability to self-sponsor through a startup means an H-1B holder laid off from a tech company now has a 60-day grace period to either find a new employer or, under the new rules, file a transfer petition through their own incorporated business — provided they have the corporate structure and specialty occupation role in place. Given the wave of tech layoffs that have disproportionately affected H-1B workers since 2023, this pathway is not theoretical. It is a live option.

Practically, founders should consult an immigration attorney experienced in entrepreneur H-1B cases before filing, establish the company's legal and financial infrastructure well in advance, and consider long-term immigration pathways — such as EB-1A (extraordinary ability), EB-2 NIW (national interest waiver), or EB-5 (investor visa) — that the startup may eventually support.
